analysis.title: The semiconductor trap
key_insights: SOX tested its longer-term trend line and range lows at Friday's lows, then closed right on the 200-day moving average. The report calls these major support levels but says the moves have been violent and the group needs more time to heal.

SOX implied volatility went from dormant to aggressively bid in a few weeks. Friday's fear was extreme across equity indices, but SOX volatility remains well below the panic levels of previous semiconductor crashes.
On the way up, SOX vol was bid as investors chased upside exposure. Now SOX vol is elevated relative to VIX because investors are buying downside protection.
SOX forward P/E has fallen to 16x, back at AI-cycle lows. The open question is whether the market has already priced a worse earnings outlook than fundamentals currently show.

Goldman data cited in the report show Korea's electronics sector accounted for roughly 60% of the country's annual GDP growth in Q3. Tech exports remain strong, machinery investment accelerated and semiconductor equipment imports kept rising, which the report reads as a reason the SOX selloff may have gone too far.
SEB X-Asset's comparison puts SOX's current pattern close to the dot-com bubble. If that roadmap holds, one more strong bounce could come before the real damage begins.

Bottom line: support, cycle-low valuations and resilient fundamentals set up a possible sharp bounce, but volatility suggests the healing is not finished. The report says cheap does not automatically mean safe.
